content.title: Institute for Global Health and Development: Webinar on Agriculture, Nutrition and Food Systems
content.summary: AKU's Institute for Global Health and Development (IGHD) completes its second webinar that is part of its Inaugural Webinar Series.

content.text: On October 28th, 2020 the Institute for Global Health and Development hosted a discussion on agriculture, nutrition, and food security that was attended by large global audience.

Dr. Howarth Bouis, co-founded of HarvestPlus, was the keynote speaker.  HarvestPlus received the World Food Prize in 2016 for accomplishments in crop biofortification. Dr. Bouis was joined by Dr. Aatekah Owais, an epidemiologist and a research fellow at the SickKids' Centre for Global Child Health who has been modeling the indirect effects of COVID-19 mitigation strategies on the health and nutrition of women, children and adolescents in South Asia. Also joining the discussion was Dr. Alex Awiti, Vice Provost, East Africa at the Aga Khan University.  His research interests intersect agriculture, climate, health policy and the economy.  Dr. Carl Amrhein, Provost and Vice President (Academic) of Aga Khan University moderated the discussion.

Dr. Bouis explained the challenges that exist in agriculture and nutrition and offered strategies to address them. People in low-income countries suffer from mineral and vitamin deficiencies because they can't afford foods such vegetables, fruits, and animal products that are high in such materials. One strategy is to increase vitamin and mineral density within staple foods through biofortification. For instance, Dr. Bouis reported on biofortified maize in Africa that was enhanced with vitamin A while maintaining an affordable market price. He described other techniques such as transgenic fortification and the use of fertilizer techniques.

Dr. Owais presented on the impact of COVID-19 in South Asia, especially as it relates to food systems and nutrition. Her research has shown that the economic impact of COVID-19 has exacerbated the economic and educational inequities seen in the region which will show compounded effects on the health and nutrition of the population. These effects will continue to be felt by the most vulnerable: women, children, and rural households. For example, 420 million school aged children have been out of school in South Asia since March 2020 and almost 9 million students will drop out. These drastic changes are estimated to result in the loss of $63.5 billion USD over the next 45 years. These values are inevitably linked to health and nutrition because a decline in GDP is associated with an increase in poverty and food insecurity in the region. Dr. Owais shared that "... even at the lowest stage of COVID 19 control measures the impact on household food insecurity is substantial with an almost 20% increase in the proportion of population experiencing food insecurity."

Dr. Awiti provided insights on food security in Arica and its determinants. Africa is the most food insecure region in the world, where 1 in 4 people are undernourished. He highlighted the yield gap. Africa has fewer irrigation systems and lower use of fertilizer compared to many other countries. He noted that imported fertilizer is expensive but there are scant local suppliers. Many challenges are intergenerational and intrinsically linked to population growth, urbanization, climate change and biodiversity loss, which is why Dr. Awiti calls for a long-term approach.
